191071:
Testimony on LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-state Advisory Council Presented by Dana Morse, Maine Sea Grant and University of Maine Cooperative Extension April 24, 2024
Dear Senator Curry, Representative Gare, and Members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee.
My name is Dana Morse. I have a joint appointment with the Maine' Sea Grant College Program, and with University of Maine Cooperative Extension. My position is Senior Extension Program Manager,
Aquaculture Lead. In this role, I undertake education, research, outreach and technology transfer
to strengthen and grow Maine's marine economy and it is with this experience that I write to share my observations on the Maine Aomori Sister State Advisory Council (MASSAC).
What I can tell you is this: the MASSAC has had a real impact on my professionalwork, and has been centralto the development of industry and science related to sea scallops, squid and now urchins as well. My first involvement lay back in 1999, when I participated in a trip to Aomori
Prefecture as part of a delegation from Maine, to study first-hand their techniques of scallop spat
collection, stock enhancement, processing and to some degree- aquaculture. That exposure, learning and suite of professional connections bore fruit not only over the next years as Maine saw a
very active network of fishermen and scientists deploying spat collectors and doing re-seeding
work, but it laid the foundation for what is now a small-but-growing sea scallop aquaculture sector
right here in Maine; the only one in the United States.
Since then, MASSAC has supported other exchanges, all of which have created concrete results.
We have imported first-of-its kind-in-the-US machinery for scallop farming, and have used
Japanese experience and knowledge to support the expansion of scallop farming in Maine, with
landings now at about $1 million over the last 4 years. The exchanges have directly influenced the markets and products we now sell (and can expand into) as our culture sector grows. Moreover, there are now growing fields of research into the confluence of oceanography and biology that have
benefits both in the fishery and culture sectors, and our young scientists and growers are better trained right out of the gate as a result. Our relationships with Japanese experts and equipment
suppliers means that our access to technical knowledge is exceptional; and has paid off not only herein Maine for scallops, seaweed and urchins, but also to our south for the squid industry.
Lastly, we have only begun to scratch the surface of the opportunies in other culinary uses of scallops, such as we have learned in Japan, opportunities which are enormous, considering the nearly $1 billion market in the US for scallop meats alone, and not counting any value-added
products.

I offer these brief remarks as a snapshot of what the MASSAC has supported in the past, and how
the activity of this group has resulted in benefits to Mainers and our overall economy. Thank you for the opportunity to provide this testimony and I look forward to answering your questions.
Dana Morse dana.morse@maine.edu 207.563.8186
191065:
Testimony in support of LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-state Advisory Council
Senator Curry, Representative Gere and members of the Committee on Housing and Economic
Development, my name is Don Hudson, retired President of Chewonki in Wiscasset, and a resident of
Arrowsic. I've been a member of the Maine Aomori Sister State Advisory Council since 2010, having been duly appointed by Governors Baldacci, LePage and Mills. I currently serve as the Acting Chair of
the Council.
Friend and colleague Don Nicoll introduced me to the Maine Aomori sister state relationship in March
2010 when he visited Chewonki with a delegation of energy planners from Aomori Prefecture. The delegation was interested in seeing how institutions in Maine were dealing with issues of energy
efficiency and overall energy use.
At the close of the visit and tour of our facilities, Don suggested that I join the Maine delegation scheduled to travel to Japan in October 2010. And so it began!
Our visit in 2010 had three purposes: to encourage and support educational exchanges, to explore aquaculture in Aomori, and to explore large-scale renewable energy efforts in the prefecture. Members of our delegation visited a marine biology research facility as well as the North Japan Research Institute for
Sustainable Energy (NJRISE) at Hirosaki University. When we returned to Maine, we set in motion a return visit of NJRISE to the Maine Tidal Power Project at the University of Maine in Orono, and several
of us also began regular `virtual' exchanges with Aomori friends and colleagues working in scallop
aquaculture. The visit to UMO was followed by visits in 2012 and 2013 and a formal collaborative
agreement between Hirosaki University and the University of Maine, focused on ocean energy, as well as
a pilot project using Ocean Renewable Power Company's tidal current turbines in Muzu Bay, Aomori.
Suffice it to say, the scallop collaboration has taken off in Maine, and fellow MASSAC member Hugh Cowperthwaite will highlight the 2016 delegation visit co-led by MASSAC, CEI, and U Maine Sea Grant
Extension.
It goes without saying that the educational and cultural exchanges, exemplified by the Maine Aomori Print Society projects over the past decade, provide opportunities for Maine people----especially students--to have a first-hand experience with Japanese culture and people. The Maine Aomori collaboration is one of Maine's most abiding international relationships. Triggered by tragedy, it has survived since October 1889---through the turmoil of global war, nurtured by individuals and communities, and for the past 30 years by our state and prefectural govemments.
If this legislation moves forward, the Maine Aomori relationship will move back to the Maine
International Trade Center where it began informally in 1995, but this time with the authority of statute, a modest budget, and the assistance of the Friends of Aomori. Lessons learned over the years by Maine students and teachers, artists, marine biologists, fishermen, renewable energy engineers and scientists can certainly inform all Maine's international exchanges.
I am happy to answer any questions you might have.
10045211:
Testimony in Support of LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory Council
Eliza Carter, eliza.carter1996@gmail.com
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and Members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development:
My name is Eliza Carter, and I am a resident of Camden, Maine. I am writing in strong support of LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory Council.
This legislation is deeply personal to me and my family. Growing up in rural Maine, we had few opportunities to engage with people from other cultures. That changed when we had the incredible privilege of hosting Japanese exchange students from Aomori two years in a row through the sister-state program. Even though our local school was not sending students to Japan at the time, the experience of welcoming those students into our home opened our eyes and hearts. We learned about their traditions, their daily lives, and their perspectives. What started as a brief visit became a lasting bond -- we remained pen pals for years after, continuing to share stories and learn from one another.
When my younger brother reached 8th grade, the program resumed at our school, and he was able to travel to Aomori himself. That journey was transformative for him -- it sparked a lifelong interest in learning about the world beyond our borders and laid the foundation for his curiosity and personal growth.
More recently, my mom and sister had the opportunity to visit Aomori, where they connected even more deeply with the culture through my sister's partner's family, who are from the region. Their experience reaffirmed what we already knew: the Maine-Aomori connection is not just about travel -- it's about deep, meaningful relationships that promote mutual understanding.
Our family's story is just one example of how this sister-state relationship fosters cultural exchange, curiosity, and empathy. These experiences have shaped our lives and our worldview, and I know countless other Maine families have been touched in similar ways.
Establishing the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory Council in statute will ensure this vital connection continues to thrive for future generations. It is a powerful reminder that even in small, rural communities like ours, we are part of a much larger global community -- and there is so much we can learn from one another.
I urge you to support LD 1336 so that this meaningful relationship between Maine and Aomori can continue to grow, enrich lives, and promote global understanding. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Testimony of Representative Ellie Sato presenting
LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-state Advisory
Council
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development
Good afternoon, Senator Cuny, Representative Gere, and esteemed members of the Joint
Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development. My name is Ellie Sato, and I represent House District 109, which includes part of Gorham. I'm proud to present LD 1336, An
Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-state Advisory Council.
This bill puts the existing Maine Aomori Sister State Advisory Council (MASSAC) in statute.
MASSAC was first established by Govemor King in 2001 by executive order to support the
ongoing sister city relationship between Bath and Tsugaru, located in the prefecture of Aomori, in Japan. This council, with the support of the nonprofit Friends of Aomori, have maintained a
strong relationship between the two cities for many years, mainly through educational and
cultural exchanges. Every two years, Bath and Tsugaru would alternate sending delegations to their respective sister city to continue to nurture the partnership, which paused during the
COVID-19 pandemic.
Relying on consecutive executive orders as administrations change puts the longevity of this relationship at serious risk. Moving the guiding documents from executive order to statute would ensure better sustainability and adaptability for the Council, allowing for greater opportunities for economic development and cultural exchange through this existing partnership.
I'm not from Bath, however, I've seen firsthand the benefits that come from Japan-Maine exchanges. For those who don't know, my father is one of the co-founders of Yosaku Restaurant in Portland. Not that I'm biased, but I do think that Yosaku Restaurant is one of the best-if not
the best--sushi restaurants in Maine.
District 109: Gorham (part)

My father's contributions to our local economy go far beyond this restaurant alone. He first
moved to the United States in l972 to help open a restaurant in San Jose. He later moved to Ohama, Nebraska to open a secondary restaurant of the same name. In the late l980's, he moved
to Maine where he helped his cousin, Yoshi Hayashi, open Sapporo Restaurant in Portland. The
general manager of the restaurant in Nebraska followed him to Maine, eventually opening his
own seafood business, called ISF Trading. ISF Trading has become a destination for many in the
Asian-American community throughout New England, as well as an important vendor for many
`
restaurants in Maine.

Now in my father's retirement, he has started a new business that truly showcases the opportunities that can come from Japan-Maine exchanges. Before the pandemic, my father
brought a group of fanners from Aurora Farm in Houlton, to Hokkaido, Japan to meet with
Japanese farmers, and learn how they grow buckwheat. Hokkaido and Maine have very similar climates, so Aurora Farm returned to Maine with Japanese buckwheat seed, and now produces
buckwheat. My father purchases their buckwheat and mills it into buckwheat flour, to sell to
Japanese restaurants across the country, who make their own soba, a traditional Japanese noodle

dish.

.

This story is just one of several exchanges that positively impact our agriculture and aquaculture industries here in Maine. Supporting the Council allows for us to sustain the foundation that the Bath/Tsugaru sister city relationship has laid for more opportunities in the future.

Before you, there is a sponsor's amendment that includes changes that address the concerns we
have heard thus far. The amendment decreases the number of members from 14 to l0 to allow for growth as the Council evolves. In a similar vein, the Council would be required to report back to the Governor, as well as the Legislature's committee of jurisdiction in case statutory changes need to be made.

The bill does request a general fund appropriation of $20,000 to support the activities of the
Council. Given the current budget climate, I understand the difficult decisions we all face.
However, this is an important investment in this partnership due to the economic development
potential and mutual benefit in fostering our continued Japan-Maine exchanges. We have an
opportunity to help support the economic development of our state, and I urge you to vote Ought
to Pass on LD 1336.

Thank you for your consideration, and I would be happy to answer any questions.

District 109: Gorham (part)

191066:
Testimony in Support of LD 1336 Emily Stowers, Farmingdale Resident
Good afternoon, my name is Emily Stowers and I'm from Farmingdale. l'm here to voice my strong support for LD 1336.
Maine has been incredibly fortunate to share a special friendship with Aomori,
Japan, for over 135 years. This relationship began in 1889, when a merchant ship
from Bath wrecked off Aomori's coast, and local residents heroically rescued four sailors. That act of kindness sparked a lasting bond that continues to grow today.
When I was 17-years-old 20 years ago I participated in a 2 week cultural exchange
with Misawa High School in Aomori through Hall-Dale high school. It was a lifechanging experience and the memories I have from that experience I will cherish forever. The emotional and personal connections that form through cultural exchanges are invaluable. These exchanges foster a sense of global community,
reminding us that despite our differences, we all share a common humanity. When we take the time to understand and respect one another's culture, we
create a more peaceful and connected world.
Through numerous cultural exchange programs--between students, artists, and communities--this relationship has enriched lives across Maine. These exchanges broaden perspectives, build respect, and help our young people prepare for a
global future.
LD 1336 is important because it strengthens that legacy. It supports education, cultural understanding, and even economic opportunities. Japan is an important
trade partner for Maine, and deeper ties can lead to more collaboration and
investment.
But beyond the practical benefits, these connections remind us of our shared humanity. They help build a world where empathy, learning, and peace are
possible.
Thank you for supporting LD 1336 and for helping keep Maine's friendship with Japan strong.
10045201:
Testimony in Support of LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory Council
Helen Carter Camden, Maine
Dear Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development,
My name is Helen Carter, and I'm from Camden, Maine. I'm here to express my support for LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory Council.
My first experience with Aomori came through a middle school exchange program. Through the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Program, I had the chance to host a student from Aomori, and that experience had a huge impact on me. Growing up in a small town in Maine, that kind of cultural connection wasn't something we came across every day. Hosting a student opened my eyes to a new way of life--and it wasn't just me. My sisters also hosted students, and eventually, my younger brother was able to visit Aomori himself and stay with a host family. These early experiences ignited a sense of global curiosity that has stayed with us, encouraging us to keep exploring, learning, and connecting with people from different cultures.
But my connection with Aomori didn't end there. My partner's father is from Aomori, and over the past few years I've worked in his Japanese restaurants, learning firsthand about Japanese food, culture, and hospitality. Now, I'm preparing to open two new businesses with my partner and his family: Aomori Restaurant and Aomori Market. While both businesses will offer a range of Japanese food, we're putting a special focus on dishes and design elements from Aomori. From what's on the menu to the crafts on the walls, we want to share what makes that region unique.
That initial connection to Aomori helped lay the foundation for what would later become both a personal and professional interest in Japanese culture. It's a reminder of how meaningful these early exchanges can be.
The sister-state relationship between Maine and Aomori creates real, lasting impacts in people's lives. It encourages curiosity, cultural understanding, and even entrepreneurship. Establishing an advisory council will help ensure that these kinds of experiences remain available to future generations of Mainers.
Thank you for your time, and I encourage you to support LD 1336.

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and distinguished members of the committee, my name is

Hugh Cowperthwaite, Senior Program Director, Fisheries & Aquaculture Program
CEI, Brunswick, Maine HughCowperthwaite@ceimaine.org

Dear Senator Curry, Representative Gere and Members of the Housing and Economic Development
Committee:
My name is Hugh Cowperthwaite, I am a resident of Falmouth, and I am here to speak in support of LD 1336. I am a current member ofthe Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory Council (MASSAC), having been duly appointed by Governor Mills in May 2024.
I first learned about Aomori, Japan when I was invited to participate in a delegation to visit Aomori in October 2010 to represent Coastal Enterprises, Inc. (CEI) where I continue to be employed to this day. In my role of Senior Program Director for CEI's Fisheries and Aquaculture Program, I am always on the lookout for
opportunities for diversifying Maine's fisheries.
On the trip in 2010, our goal was to learn about Aomori's energy practices and fisheries and share our
experiences from Maine. I spent the next several days learning about Aomori's robust commercial scallop farming industry centered around Mutsu Bay. I had never seen anything like it. The people, their kindness,
care and attention to detail all in the name of seafood production - I was truly amazed and inspired.
My mind was racing, and I said to myself "we can do this in Maine" . I made friends quickly with our Japanese
hosts and began making plans to host some guests in Maine.
Since that first trip in 2010 I have helped many aquaculture and commercial fishing businesses in Maine by leveraging the opportunity I was given to visit Aomori and the contacts I've made. As a result, businesses have been launched and farmed (native) Atlantic Sea scallops are now available in Maine. There is no other farmed
scallop like it on the national market. It's unique and fetches a premium price for our Maine growers. We have
created a new fishery to help Maine's marine economy diversify.
To this day I remain connected with friends and businesses in Aomori and have branched up into Hokkaido. I
have now visited Japan four times and each time I have brought commercial fishermen and aquaculturists from Maine with me (now totaling 25 people). Learning has expanded beyond sea scallops, and we are now
learning about farmed and wild harvested kelp, seaweed and most recently sea urchins.
The Maine Aomori relationship is a treasure for our state, and we should continue to foster our international connections now more than ever. I urge your support with this modest request to create in statute the MASSAC and provide support to the Maine International Trade Center for administering the Council.

I am a professional in international education and affairs, currently sen/ing as Program
Director for the Council of American Overseas Research Centers in Washington, DC. Prior to this role, I spent 16 years as Department Chair and professor of art at Southern Maine Community College, where I launched a Global Studies Center and a study

years, curating exhibitions with a focus on international exchange.

Testimony of Senate President Mattie Daughtry in support of LD 1336, "An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-state Advisory Council"
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development
Good afternoon, Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and esteemed members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee. My name is Mattie Daughtry and I am proud to serve as the President of the Maine State Senate, where I am honored to represent Senate District 23, which includes Brunswick, Freeport, Harpswell, Pownal, Chebeague Island, and part of Yarmouth.
Since the establishment of our sister-state relationship in 1994, Maine and the Japanese province of Aomori have cultivated a collaborative bond that has yielded significant benefits, particularly in the area of aquaculture. Aquaculture is an industry my district holds dear. Aomori is renowned for its excellence in scallop farming, and Maine has been actively learning from their expertise. Techniques such as "ear hanging" have been shared with us, allowing Maine's scallop farmers to enhance their practices and increase production. This collaboration is not just about sharing methods; it's about exchanging knowledge that drives our local seafood industry's growth and innovation.Our first official delegation to Aomori in 1994 introduced us to these practices, and subsequent visits, including a fisheries-only delegation in 1997 and further delegations in 2010 and 2016, have deepened our understanding and adoption of these techniques.
The relationship between Maine and Aomori extends beyond economic collaboration. Cultural initiatives like the Maine-Aomori Printmaking Society (MAPS) have fostered art exchanges and residencies, promoting mutual cultural understanding and educational projects highlighting our sister-state connection.
As a business owner, I recognize the immense value that LD 1336 will bring. By formalizing the Maine-Aomori Sister-state Advisory Council, we create a structured way to facilitate further exchanges in aquaculture, and beyond. This council will enable more streamlined communication and collaboration, paving the way for technology transfers that can lead to remarkable advancements in local industries. Increased access to Aomori's cutting-edge equipment and techniques could allow Maine's scallop industry to thrive, producing higher quality products that meet growing market demands. Moreover, the economic impact of enhanced collaboration with Aomori cannot be overstated. By investing in our sister-state relationship through this advisory council, we lay the groundwork for future trade opportunities that could include the exchange of expertise, equipment, and potentially even fresh scallops, which are in high demand.

Let us not underestimate the potential of our relationship with Aomori. The collaboration we have experienced so far has already led to increased scallop farming in Maine, and the foundation this bill creates will only bolster future success. LD 1336 represents a commitment to investing in our local aquaculture industry and ensuring that Maine can compete and thrive in a global seafood market. I strongly urge you to support LD 1336. Testimony of Maureen Terry

LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister State Advisory Council

Senator Curry, Representative Gere and Members of the Committee on Housing and
Economic Development, my name is Mo Terry, and I am the legislative liaison for the
Department of Community and Economic Development, and I am testifying on behalf of the
Maine International Trade Center (MITC).
Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony on LD 1336, An Act to Establish the
Maine-Aomori Sister-state Advisory Council. The department is generally supportive of the Council. This sister city relationship has existed since Governor Baldacci created the Council
by Executive Order in 1994, with political and community support ebbing and flowing over the years. The council has staying power and, given the right structure, could continue its work in a more sustained function. We've reviewed the two economies for synergies and there is some potential for coordination on the ocean economy, tourism, and outdoor recreation. That said, Aomori is much like Maine, so we need to appropriately calibrate our
investment for the potential return. With this in mind, we would like to propose several considerations that may enhance the effectiveness of the Council.
First, regarding the council's composition, the proposed membership of 14 appointed
members, in addition to a member from MITC, may be too large and too prescriptive for
efficient operations. A smaller initial membership with more at large seats would allow for a
more agile group, while still ensuring diverse representation. This approach would also leave
room for future growth as the council's activities expand and evolve. We recommend reducing
the number of appointed members to a more manageable level to facilitate productive discussions and decision-making.

Second, we note that the bill contains limited language regarding economic development or
trade. Given the importance of trade and commerce to the work of the Maine International
Trade Center, we wonder if this is the most appropriate entity to house the council's activities. Tying culture, education and recreation to economic development or trade may help ensure
that these aspects receive adequate attention.
Additionally, we recommend refining the language regarding funding. Instead of stating that
the initiative "provides ongoing funds to support the Maine-Aomori Sister-state Advisory
Council," we propose revising it to "provides ongoing funds to MITC to support the activities of the group." This revision clarifies the role of MITC in administering the funds and aligns
with the intent to support the council's work effectively.
Lastly, we would like to see an operating agreement that sets clear expectations for the
council's work, responsibilities, and governance. Establishing such an agreement would ensure transparency, accountability, and a well-defined scope of activities for the council moving forward.
We appreciate this effort to formalize and support the Maine-Aomori sister-state relationship
and encourage thoughtful revisions to strengthen the bill's framework. Thank you for your
consideration, and we look forward to continued discussions on this important initiative.

Dear Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development,
My name is Reo Miyake, and I am a resident of Portland, Maine. I am here today to express my strong support for LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory Council.
I have deep personal and family ties to both Maine and Aomori, Japan. My father grew up in Aomori, and after moving to Maine 15 years ago, he felt at home right away due to the shared climate and lifestyle. As I continue to build my life here, I have been eager to learn more about my father's home that shaped him.
This past week, I had the privilege of traveling to Aomori with my parents, my partner, and her mother. We explored the region's cultural history, local crafts, and food. It was incredibly meaningful to experience the place where my father grew up and to share that connection with my family.
My parents, my partner, and I are now working to open two new businesses in Portland: Aomori Restaurant and Aomori Kitchen + Market. These ventures are inspired by the ties between Maine and the Thoku region of Japan, and we hope they will serve as spaces where people can come together and experience their shared traditions.
As someone with a deep interest in both Maine and Japan, I know firsthand how valuable cross-cultural connections can be. The establishment of the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory Council will strengthen these relationships and provide structure for future collaborations--not just in business, but in education, the arts, and community life.
I strongly urge you to support LD 1336 to help maintain and deepen this vital connection between Maine and Aomori, and to continue enriching the global perspective of our students and citizens alike.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Reo Miyake Portland, Maine
10045553:
Wilson Ball North Yarmouth, Maine
Dear Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development,
My name is Wilson Ball. I am from from North Yarmouth, Maine, and I currently reside in Tokyo, Japan. I am submitting this testimony in favor of LD 1336, An Act to Establish the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Advisory CouncilI.
My earliest interaction with Aomori was when I was in high school, when my younger brother hosted an exchange student from Aomori through the Maine-Aomori Sister-State Program. Although I was not personally involved with the program itself, I fondly remember the experience of hosting our exchange student, and as I go through my daily life in Japan, I regard it as a very influential factor in starting my interest in Japanese culture. Our exchange student was very kind, and much more considerate than I would expect any middle school-aged child to be. Before making the very long trip to Maine, he carefully read the profile that my brother had provided to the exchange program, and brought gifts for our whole family that he thought we would enjoy. He brought an origami set, small decorative paper lanterns, and daruma otoshi: a traditional Japanese game with stacking blocks. After interacting with him for the week, my curiosity for Japanese traditions and culture only grew. I believe that if not for this exchange program, I would not be where I am today: living abroad in Tokyo, studying Japanese cuisine at the Tokyo College of Sushi and Washoku (traditional Japanese cooking).
A few years ago, I had the fortune to be able to travel almost the entirety of Japan, North to South, and I learned more than I could have ever hoped to about the people, environment, values, and cultures of the country. Each region I visited felt very unique. My opinions have since been reinforced, learning in more detail the differences in the cooking styles of the regions; each distinctly shaped by the history, environment, and pride of the people living there. The prefectures all have their own strong personalities and values that express themselves through the people. I struggle to think of a personality that matches Maine's as much as that of Aomori. Independence that springs from a strong sense of resilience, consideration of others and community, and a ready willingness to help others in need are values that I very definitively feel from both Maine and Aomori.
Although I do currently live in the metropolis of Tokyo, in the event that I decide to continue living in Japan I can hardly imagine a single place in the country that evokes such familiar feelings of home as much as Aomori. I believe the establishment of an advisory council will help other people experience this home they have on the other side of the planet, and foster a community with the potential to span generations.
Thank you for your consideration. I encourage you to support LD 1336.
